chem_ocra.13.2.summary: Catalysts are substances that increase the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed at the end of the process. They work by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, meaning a greater proportion of colliding particles possess the minimum energy required to react successfully. Reaction profiles visually represent these energy changes, allowing us to compare catalysed and uncatalysed pathways for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.

core.p: A catalyst is a chemical substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction. Crucially, it remains chemically unchanged and unconsumed at the end of the reaction, meaning it can be recovered and reused indefinitely.
bullets: Increases the rate of reaction significantly
Remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction
Is not used up; mass at start equals mass at end
Does not alter the overall amount of products formed
Only a very small amount of catalyst is usually required

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction, without being used up or chemically changed by the end of the reaction.

core.p: Catalysts do not increase the collision frequency between reactant particles. Instead, they change the mechanism of the reaction entirely by providing an alternative reaction pathway that requires less energy.
bullets: Provides an alternative reaction pathway
Involves different steps or intermediates
Lowers the activation energy barrier
Does not change the energy of reactants or products
Does not change the overall enthalpy change (Delta H)

callouts.p: Catalysts work by lowering activation energy through an alternative pathway, not by increasing particle speed or collision frequency.

core.p: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must collide with in order for a chemical reaction to occur. By lowering this threshold, more collisions become successful.
bullets: Activation energy is abbreviated as Ea
Higher activation energy means fewer successful collisions
A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Ea)
A greater proportion of particles now have energy greater than or equal to the new lower Ea
Frequency of successful collisions increases, increasing the rate of reaction

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide in order for a chemical reaction to take place.

core.p: Reaction profiles are graphical representations that show how the energy of reactants and products changes during the course of a chemical reaction. They display energy on the vertical axis and progress of reaction on the horizontal axis.
bullets: Y-axis represents energy (kJ or kJ/mol)
X-axis represents progress of reaction or time
Reactants are plotted on the left-hand side
Products are plotted on the right-hand side
Peak represents the transition state or activation energy barrier

core.p: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released to the surroundings. The products have less energy than the reactants, resulting in a negative enthalpy change (Delta H).
bullets: Reactants start higher on the Y-axis than products
Overall energy change (Delta H) is negative
Curve rises to a peak representing activation energy from reactants
Curve falls below the reactant level to reach products
Surroundings warm up as energy is released

callouts.p: Products are lower in energy than reactants, showing energy has been released to the surroundings.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an exothermic reaction showing the uncatalysed pathway and lower activation energy catalysed alternative pathway.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M 50 180 L 100 80 L 150 120" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 100 80 L 120 110 L 150 120" fill="none" stroke="#e11d48" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><line x1="50" y1="180" x2="350" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="20" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Energy</text><text x="180" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Progress of reaction</text><text x="55" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Reactants</text><text x="260" y="125" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Products</text><text x="95" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Uncatalysed peak</text><text x="110" y="102" font-size="11" fill="#e11d48">Catalysed peak</text></svg>

core.p: In an endothermic reaction, energy is absorbed from the surroundings. The products have more energy than the reactants, resulting in a positive enthalpy change (Delta H).
bullets: Reactants start lower on the Y-axis than products
Overall energy change (Delta H) is positive
Curve rises steeply to a high peak activation energy
Curve descends to products that sit higher than reactants
Surroundings cool down as energy is absorbed

callouts.p: Products are higher in energy than reactants, showing energy has been absorbed from the surroundings.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an endothermic reaction, illustrating how the catalyst lowers the peak without changing reactant or product energy levels.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M 50 160 L 130 50 L 220 110" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 130 50 L 160 85 L 220 110" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><line x1="50" y1="190" x2="350" y2="190" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="20" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Energy</text><text x="180" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Progress of reaction</text><text x="55" y="155" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Reactants</text><text x="230" y="105" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Products</text><text x="125" y="42" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Uncatalysed peak</text><text x="145" y="78" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">Catalysed peak</text></svg>

core.p: On a reaction profile diagram, the catalysed reaction path is shown by an alternative curve that has a lower maximum peak than the uncatalysed reaction path.
bullets: Uncatalysed path shown with a solid line and high peak
Catalysed path shown with a dashed or lower solid line
Peak for catalysed path is clearly lower than uncatalysed peak
Start point (reactants) and end point (products) remain identical
Distance from reactants to peak represents activation energy (Ea)

callouts.p: Always start and end the catalysed curve at the exact same heights as the uncatalysed curve. Only the peak height changes.

core.p: Activation energy is measured on a reaction profile as the vertical energy difference between the energy level of the reactants and the highest point (peak) of the curve.
bullets: Measure from reactant line up to the top of the curve peak
Uncatelysed Ea is the distance from reactants to the main peak
Catalysed Ea is the distance from reactants to the lower catalysed peak
Lower Ea value indicates faster reaction rate
Units are typically kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol)

core.h: Identifying Enthalpy Change (Delta H) on Profiles
core.p: The overall enthalpy change of a reaction is represented on a reaction profile by the vertical distance between the energy level of the reactants and the energy level of the products.
bullets: Measure from reactant line horizontally across to product level
Negative Delta H for exothermic (products lower than reactants)
Positive Delta H for endothermic (products higher than reactants)
Catalysts do not change Delta H
Do not confuse Delta H with activation energy

callouts.p: Students often mix up activation energy (reactants to peak) and enthalpy change (reactants to products). Check your definitions.

core.h: Types of Catalysts: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
core.p: Catalysts can be classified based on whether they are in the same physical state as the reactants or in a different state.
bullets: Homogeneous catalysts are in the same physical state as the reactants (e.g. all aqueous)
Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different physical state from the reactants (e.g. solid catalyst, gas reactants)
Transition metals and their compounds are excellent heterogeneous catalysts
Enzymes are complex biological homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysts in living systems
Heterogeneous catalysts often work by providing a surface for reactant molecules to adsorb onto

core.p: Catalysts are vital in industrial chemistry because they save money, reduce energy consumption, and increase production efficiency.
bullets: Allow reactions to take place at lower temperatures
Reduce energy demands and fuel costs for heating
Increase the rate of production per unit time
Can make previously uneconomical industrial processes viable
Examples include iron in the Haber process and platinum/rhodium in catalytic converters

callouts.p: Lower temperatures needed with catalysts mean less fossil fuels burned, reducing both costs and carbon footprint.

analogy.p: Imagine hikers trying to travel from one valley to another. Without a catalyst, they must climb right over the highest, steepest peak of the mountain range (the uncatalysed activation energy). A catalyst builds a tunnel straight through the lower part of the mountain (the alternative pathway with lower activation energy). Much less effort and energy is needed to cross, so many more hikers make the journey successfully in less time, while the mountain itself remains unchanged at the end. This breaks down because real reactant particles do not consciously choose routes; rather, the catalyst alters the chemical bonding pathways available.

terms.d: A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed.
The minimum amount of energy colliding particles must have to react.
A graph showing the energy changes during the course of a reaction from reactants to products.
A reaction that releases energy to the surroundings, resulting in products with less energy than reactants.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, resulting in products with more energy than reactants.
The overall change in thermal energy during a reaction, denoted as Delta H.
A different route for a chemical reaction that has a lower activation energy.
A catalyst that is in the same physical state as the reactants.
A catalyst that is in a different physical state from the reactants.
Elements from the central block of the periodic table, many of which act as effective catalysts.
A collision between particles that results in a reaction because particles have energy equal to or greater than activation energy.
The high-energy state corresponding to the peak of the activation energy barrier.

mistakes.w: A catalyst gets used up in the reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst is chemically unchanged and remains at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: A catalyst increases the total yield of a reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst only increases the rate of reaction; it does not change the amount of product formed.

mistakes.w: A catalyst provides energy to the particles.
mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, it does not add thermal energy.

mistakes.w: A catalyst changes the overall enthalpy change (Delta H).
mistakes.r: Delta H is determined solely by the energy of reactants and products, which remains unchanged by a catalyst.

mistakes.w: Activation energy is measured from the products to the peak.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak.

mistakes.w: Catalysts increase the speed of reactant particles.
mistakes.r: Particle speed is determined by temperature, not catalysts. Catalysts lower activation energy.
Homogeneous catalysts are in the same state as reactants (e.g. aqueous or liquid), whereas solid catalysts are usually heterogeneous.

exam.q: Define what is meant by the term 'catalyst'.
model: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction
And is not used up / remains chemically unchanged at the end
exam.tip: Both marking points are essential for full marks.

exam.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
model: Provides an alternative reaction pathway
That has a lower activation energy
So a greater proportion of particles have energy exceeding the activation energy / more successful collisions
exam.tip: Mentioning lower activation energy and alternative pathway secures standard examiner points.

exam.q: State whether a catalyst changes the overall energy change (Delta H) of a reaction.
model: No
exam.tip: Keep direct answers short for 1-mark recall questions.

exam.q: Describe how activation energy is represented on a reaction profile diagram.
model: The vertical distance
From the energy level of the reactants to the peak of the curve
exam.tip: Be precise with starting and ending points.

exam.q: A student draws a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction. On the same axes, draw and label the curve for the catalysed reaction.
model: Curve starts and ends at the exact same energy levels as the uncatalysed curve
Peak of the new curve is clearly lower than the original peak
exam.tip: Ensure your curve starts and finishes level with the original reactants and products.

exam.q: Explain why using a catalyst can reduce industrial heating costs.
model: Catalysts lower the activation energy
Allowing reactions to be run at lower temperatures while maintaining rate
exam.tip: Link lower activation energy directly to reduced temperature and fuel usage.

exam.q: Distinguish between a homogeneous catalyst and a heterogeneous catalyst.
model: Homogeneous catalyst is in the same physical state as the reactants
Heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state from the reactants
exam.tip: Use terms like 'physical state' or 'phase'.

exam.q: State one reason why transition metals are widely used as catalysts.
model: They make effective heterogeneous catalysts / they have variable oxidation states / they readily adsorb reactant molecules
exam.tip: Accept any valid property of transition metals acting as catalysts.

exam.q: Explain why adding a catalyst does not alter the amount of product formed in a batch reaction.
model: Catalysts only affect the rate of reaction
The amount of product is determined solely by the mass and moles of limiting reactants
exam.tip: Distinguish clearly between rate (how fast) and yield (how much).

worked.q: Use the reaction profile data to calculate the activation energy for the uncatalysed and catalysed reactions given: Reactants = 50 kJ/mol, Products = 20 kJ/mol, Uncatalysed peak = 130 kJ/mol, Catalysed peak = 90 kJ/mol.
steps: Identify the energy of the reactants: 50 kJ/mol.
Find the uncatalysed activation energy by subtracting reactant energy from the uncatalysed peak: 130 - 50 = 80 kJ/mol.
Find the catalysed activation energy by subtracting reactant energy from the catalysed peak: 90 - 50 = 40 kJ/mol.
worked.ans: Uncatalysed Ea = 80 kJ/mol; Catalysed Ea = 40 kJ/mol.

worked.q: Explain how the reaction profile for an endothermic reaction changes when a catalyst is added, referencing activation energy and enthalpy change.
steps: State that the reactant and product energy levels remain unchanged, so overall Delta H is unaffected.
Identify that the peak of the curve representing the activation energy is lower on the catalysed profile.
Conclude that the alternative pathway lowers the activation energy from reactants to the peak.
worked.ans: The reactant and product levels stay the same (positive Delta H unchanged), but the peak height is reduced, showing a lower activation energy.

chem_ocra.13.1.summary: Chemical reactions occur at vastly different speeds, and understanding collision theory allows us to control these rates precisely. By manipulating temperature, concentration, pressure, and surface area, we alter the frequency and energy of collisions between reacting particles. Mastering these factors explains how particles interact on a microscopic scale to determine macroscopic reaction speeds.

core.p: The rate of a chemical reaction is a measure of how quickly reactants are used up or how quickly products are formed. To control reactions in industrial processes and laboratory settings, we must understand the fundamental theory that explains how and why chemical changes occur.
bullets: **Rate of reaction** measures the speed at which a reaction takes place.
Can be measured by monitoring the disappearance of reactants or formation of products.
Fast reactions like explosions happen almost instantaneously.
Slow reactions like the rusting of iron take years.

callouts.p: Chemical reactions only happen when particles collide with enough energy.

core.p: Collision theory states that chemical reactions can only occur when reacting particles collide with each other. However, not every collision results in a chemical change; most collisions just cause particles to bounce off each other without reacting.
bullets: Particles must collide to react.
Most collisions are **unsuccessful** because particles lack sufficient energy.
Only a small fraction of total collisions lead to a reaction at room conditions.
Successful collisions require specific geometric orientation and sufficient energy.

callouts.p: A theory that states chemical reactions occur only when reacting particles collide with sufficient energy.

fig.cap: Comparison of unsuccessful and successful particle collisions based on energy and orientation.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="230" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="100" y="25" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Unsuccessful Collision</text><text x="300" y="25" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Successful Collision</text><circle cx="70" cy="100" r="20" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="70" y="104" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">A</text><circle cx="130" cy="100" r="20" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="130" y="104" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">B</text><line x1="95" y1="100" x2="105" y2="100" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="100" y="145" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#475569">Low Energy Bounce</text><circle cx="270" cy="100" r="20" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><text x="270" y="104" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">A</text><circle cx="330" cy="100" r="20" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><text x="330" y="104" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">B</text><line x1="295" y1="100" x2="305" y2="100" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 285 130 Q 300 150 315 130" fill="none" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300" y="180" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#166534">Forms Products</text></svg>

core.p: For particles to react upon colliding, they must overcome an energy barrier known as the activation energy. This is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react when they collide.
bullets: **Activation energy (Ea)** is the minimum kinetic energy required for a collision to be successful.
Reactions with high activation energies are very slow at room temperature.
Particles with energy below Ea will simply bounce off each other unchanged.
Providing heat increases the proportion of particles with energy equal to or greater than Ea.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy needed for particles to react when they collide.

core.p: The rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the frequency of successful collisions between reactant particles. Anything that increases the number of successful collisions per second will increase the rate of reaction.
bullets: **Collision frequency** is the number of collisions per unit time.
Successful collision frequency determines the overall rate of reaction.
Increasing particle speed increases collision frequency.
Increasing particle crowding increases collision frequency.

callouts.p: Always use the phrase 'frequency of successful collisions' rather than just 'more collisions' to secure full marks.

core.p: Increasing the temperature of a reaction mixture increases the rate of reaction significantly. This happens because thermal energy is transferred to the particles, making them move much faster.
bullets: Particles gain **kinetic energy** and move faster when heated.
Higher speed means collisions happen more frequently.
More importantly, a much larger fraction of particles now have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
A small increase in temperature can cause a large increase in rate.

callouts.p: Do not just say 'particles move faster so they collide more'. You must also state that they collide with *more energy* exceeding the activation energy.

fig.cap: Effect of temperature on particle speed and energy distribution.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="200" y="25" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Particle Kinetic Energy Distribution</text><path d="M 40 200 Q 120 40 200 200" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 80 200 Q 160 80 240 200" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="230" y1="50" x2="230" y2="210" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="3"/><text x="235" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Activation Energy</text><text x="110" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">Lower Temp</text><text x="180" y="100" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">Higher Temp</text><line x1="40" y1="210" x2="360" y2="210" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#64748b">Particle Kinetic Energy</text></svg>

core.p: Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution means there are more reactant particles packed into the same volume of solvent. This increases the crowding of particles, leading to more frequent collisions.
bullets: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume.
Particles are closer together on average.
The **frequency of successful collisions** increases.
Rate of reaction is higher at the start and decreases as reactants are used up.

callouts.p: Doubling the concentration doubles the frequency of successful collisions, doubling the initial rate.

fig.cap: Visualising low versus high concentration in solution.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="40" y="40" width="130" height="150" rx="5" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="230" y="40" width="130" height="150" rx="5" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="2"/><text x="105" y="30" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Low Concentration</text><text x="295" y="30" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">High Concentration</text><circle cx="70" cy="70" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="130" cy="90" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="90" cy="140" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="140" cy="160" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="250" cy="60" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="280" cy="80" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="260" cy="110" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="310" cy="120" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="340" cy="150" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="270" cy="170" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><circle cx="320" cy="180" r="8" fill="#0284c7"/><text x="105" y="215" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#475569">Few collisions per second</text><text x="295" y="215" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#475569">More collisions per second</text></svg>

core.p: For gases, changing the pressure has a similar effect to changing concentration in solutions. Increasing the pressure pushes gas molecules into a smaller volume, increasing how closely packed they are.
bullets: Applies only to **gases**.
Higher pressure compresses the gas into a smaller volume.
Gas particles are closer together.
Frequency of successful collisions increases, raising the rate of reaction.

callouts.p: Decreasing container volume increases pressure, which increases rate.

core.h: Effect of Surface Area on Rate
core.p: When a solid reactant is broken down into smaller pieces, or powdered, its surface area increases. Only the particles on the outside surface can collide with reactant particles in solution or gas.
bullets: Smaller pieces have a much larger **surface area to volume ratio**.
More reactant particles are exposed to attack.
Frequency of successful collisions increases.
Lumps react slowly; powders react rapidly.

callouts.p: The total area of reactant exposed to colliding particles.

fig.cap: Comparing surface area of a large solid block versus divided smaller pieces.

core.p: Graphs of rate data show how the amount of reactant or product changes over time. The steeper the gradient of the line on a rate graph, the faster the reaction is proceeding at that point.
bullets: Steeper line = **faster rate of reaction**.
Line becomes horizontal when the reaction is complete (limiting reactant used up).
Higher temperature or concentration gives a steeper initial curve.
Total volume of product formed depends on moles of limiting reactant, not rate.

callouts.p: Gradient equals rate; change in y divided by change in x.

core.p: Students must know how to measure rates of reaction experimentally. Common methods include measuring gas volume produced using a gas syringe, measuring mass loss as gas escapes, or noting colour changes/precipitation.
bullets: Magnesium with hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen gas measured via gas syringe.
Calcium carbonate with acid produces carbon dioxide measured by mass loss on a balance.
Sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid form a sulfur precipitate, obscuring a black cross.
Always control variables such as volume, concentration, and temperature.

head: Method
Apparatus
Measurement
rows: Loss of mass as gas escapes

callouts.p: When investigating surface area, keep mass of solid, volume of acid, and temperature constant.

core.p: At Higher tier, collision energy distribution is often explained using energy distribution curves. This graph shows the proportion of molecules possessing different kinetic energies at a given temperature.
bullets: Area under the curve represents the total number of particles.
Activation energy marks the threshold for successful collisions.
Raising temperature shifts the peak to the right and lowers it.
The area under the curve beyond the activation energy increases significantly when heated.

callouts.p: A graph showing the distribution of kinetic energies among molecules in a gas or liquid.

analogy.p: Imagine a dance floor where couples are trying to bump into each other and high-five. If you turn up the music and make everyone dance faster (temperature), or cram twice as many dancers onto the floor (concentration/pressure), or break big dance circles into solo dancers so everyone has more exposed edges (surface area), people will bump into each other much more often. Where it breaks down: dancer collisions do not require a specific activation energy barrier to succeed like chemical bonds do.

terms.d: A measure of how fast a reactant is used up or how fast a product is formed.
A model stating that chemical reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy.
The minimum energy needed for particles to react upon collision.
The number of collisions between particles per unit time.
A collision that results in a chemical reaction because particles have enough energy.
The number of reactant particles present in a given volume of solution.
A measure of how tightly packed gas molecules are within a given container volume.
The total area of a solid reactant exposed to surrounding liquid or gas reactants.
The reactant that is completely used up first, stopping the reaction.
The steepness of a graph line, representing the rate of reaction at that point.
The energy an object possesses due to its motion.
An insoluble solid formed in a solution during a chemical reaction.

mistakes.w: Particles move faster so they collide more.
mistakes.r: You must also state they collide with more energy exceeding activation energy.

mistakes.w: Increasing surface area creates more particles.
mistakes.r: Surface area exposes more existing particles to contact with other reactants.

mistakes.w: Higher temperature gives particles more activation energy.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is fixed; temperature gives particles more kinetic energy to meet that barrier.
Concentration increases collision frequency, not collision strength.

mistakes.w: Pressure affects solids and liquids in reactions.
mistakes.r: Pressure only significantly affects the rate of reactions involving gases.

mistakes.w: Catalysts increase the final yield of a reaction.
mistakes.r: Catalysts speed up the rate of reaction but do not change the total amount of product.

exam.q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a chemical reaction. (4 marks)
model: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
This increases the frequency of successful collisions.
A greater proportion of particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
More collisions result in a reaction per second.
exam.tip: Make sure to mention both increased frequency and increased energy exceeding activation energy.

exam.q: Explain why magnesium powder reacts much faster with hydrochloric acid than a magnesium ribbon of the same mass. (3 marks)
model: Powder has a larger surface area to volume ratio.
More particles are exposed to the acid.
This leads to a higher frequency of successful collisions.
exam.tip: Always link surface area changes directly to collision frequency.

exam.q: Describe the effect of increasing concentration on the rate of reaction in terms of particles. (2 marks)
model: There are more particles per unit volume in solution.
This increases the frequency of successful collisions.
exam.tip: Keep explanations concise for 2-mark questions focusing on particle crowding.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term 'activation energy'. (1 mark)
model: The minimum energy required for particles to react upon collision.
exam.tip: Learn definitions word-for-word as mark schemes are strict.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of reaction usually decreases as time goes on. (2 marks)
model: Reactant particles are used up as the reaction proceeds.
There are fewer reactant particles per unit volume, reducing collision frequency.
exam.tip: Link decreasing rate directly to decreasing reactant concentration over time.

exam.q: Explain how increasing gas pressure increases the rate of reaction. (3 marks)
model: Gas molecules are compressed into a smaller volume.
Particles are closer together on average.
This leads to an increased frequency of successful collisions.
exam.tip: Reference volume and particle proximity for full marks.

exam.q: Draw a labelled diagram showing how to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction over time. (3 marks)
model: Conical flask containing reactants with a bung and delivery tube.
Gas syringe connected to collect gas.
Labels correctly identifying flask, delivery tube, and gas syringe.
exam.tip: Ensure airtight connections are implied in apparatus setups.

exam.q: A student investigates the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid. State two variables that must be kept constant to make it a fair test. (2 marks)
model: Concentration of hydrochloric acid.
Volume of hydrochloric acid / mass of marble chips / temperature.
exam.tip: Choose easy-to-control variables such as volume or concentration.

exam.q: Explain why most collisions between reactant particles do not result in a reaction. (2 marks)
model: Particles collide with less energy than the activation energy.
Particles may also collide with incorrect orientation.
exam.tip: Mention both energy and orientation for comprehensive credit.

worked.q: Calculate the average rate of reaction between 0 and 30 seconds if 45 cm3 of hydrogen gas is produced.
steps: Identify the formula: Rate = Change in volume / Change in time.
Substitute the values: 45 cm3 divided by 30 s.
Calculate the final value and include correct units.

worked.q: A reaction loses 2.4 g of carbon dioxide gas in 40 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss.
steps: Identify the formula: Rate = Mass lost / Time taken.
Substitute the values: 2.4 g divided by 40 s.

chem_ocra.13.3.summary: Enzymes are specialized biological catalysts produced by living cells to speed up vital metabolic reactions without being consumed or permanently altered during the process. They possess highly specific three-dimensional active sites that bind exclusively to complementary substrates through the lock and key mechanism. Understanding enzyme structure, function, and factors like temperature and pH is essential for mastering organic chemistry, biochemistry, and industrial biotechnology applications.

core.p: Enzymes are large proteins made up of long chains of amino acids folded into complex three-dimensional shapes. They act as biological catalysts in all living organisms, speeding up chemical reactions that would otherwise occur too slowly to sustain life.
bullets: Proteins folded into precise 3D structures.
Function as biological catalysts in living organisms.
Speed up metabolic reactions without being used up.
Operate efficiently at body temperature under mild conditions.

callouts.p: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that increases the rate of metabolic reactions by lowering the activation energy.

core.p: Every enzyme molecule contains a very specific region called the active site. The shape and chemical properties of this active site are uniquely tailored to fit only one specific reactant molecule, known as the substrate.
bullets: Active site is a specialized cleft or pocket on the enzyme surface.
Shape of the active site is complementary to a specific substrate.
Non-matching substrates cannot bind to the active site.
Determined by the precise sequence of amino acids in the protein chain.

callouts.p: The specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the catalytic reaction takes place.

fig.cap: Diagram showing an enzyme with a distinct active site shape waiting to bind a complementary substrate molecule.

core.p: The lock and key model explains how enzymes work with extreme specificity. The substrate fits precisely into the enzyme's active site just like a specific key fits into a unique lock, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
bullets: Substrate approaches the enzyme active site.
Substrate collides and binds perfectly into the active site.
Forms a temporary enzyme-substrate complex.
Reaction occurs rapidly, converting substrate into products.

callouts.p: Always state that the active site is complementary in shape to the substrate.

fig.cap: The lock and key model illustrating enzyme-substrate complex formation.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><path d="M60 70 Q100 40 140 70 Q180 100 190 150 Q140 190 90 150 Z" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e3a8a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M210 90 Q240 90 240 120 Q240 150 210 150 Z" fill="#fef08a" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M260 110 L280 130 L260 150" fill="none" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="240" y1="120" x2="255" y2="120" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="125" fill="#1e3a8a" font-size="12">Enzyme</text><text x="215" y="125" fill="#713f12" font-size="11">Substrate</text><text x="120" y="30" fill="#0f172a" font-size="13">Enzyme-Substrate Complex Formation</text></svg>

core.p: Once the chemical reaction is complete inside the active site, the products are released because their shape no longer fits the active site. The enzyme remains entirely unchanged and can immediately catalyze another reaction.
bullets: Products depart from the active site.
Enzyme returns to its original, unchanged state.
Single enzyme molecule can process thousands of substrate molecules per second.
Enzymes are not consumed during the reaction.

callouts.p: Enzymes are regenerated at the end of the reaction and are not used up.

core.p: Because active sites have unique shapes, each enzyme usually catalyzes only one specific reaction or type of reaction. For example, amylase breaks down starch into sugars, but it cannot break down proteins or fats.
bullets: High degree of reaction specificity.
One enzyme works for one specific substrate.
Protease enzymes break down proteins, lipase breaks down fats.
Mismatched substrates cannot bind, so no reaction occurs.

callouts.p: Do not say 'enzymes break down food'. Name the specific enzyme and its corresponding substrate.

core.h: Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity
core.p: As temperature increases, enzyme and substrate particles gain kinetic energy, moving faster and colliding more frequently. This increases the rate of reaction up to an optimum temperature, after which the enzyme denatures.
bullets: Rate increases with temperature up to the optimum point.
Optimum temperature is typically around 37 degrees Celsius in humans.
Higher kinetic energy leads to more successful collisions per second.
Excessive heat breaks bonds holding the protein structure together.

callouts.p: The temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum possible rate.

core.p: If the temperature becomes too high or the pH strays too far from the optimum, the weak bonds holding the enzyme's 3D structure break. This permanently changes the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer fit.
bullets: Active site shape is permanently altered or destroyed.
Substrate can no longer bind to the active site.
Catalytic activity stops completely.
Denaturation is irreversible under normal biological conditions.

callouts.p: Describes an enzyme whose active site shape has changed permanently due to extreme heat or pH, stopping substrate binding.

fig.cap: Normal functional enzyme active site compared to a denatured enzyme with a distorted shape.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><path d="M80 80 Q120 50 160 80 Q200 110 200 150 Q120 180 80 150 Z" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M260 80 Q290 40 340 90 Q320 140 250 160 Z" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="120" fill="#166534" font-size="11">Normal Active Site</text><text x="270" y="120" fill="#991b1b" font-size="11">Denatured Shape</text><text x="120" y="30" fill="#0f172a" font-size="13">Normal vs Denatured Enzyme Structure</text></svg>

core.h: Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity
core.p: Different enzymes have different optimum pH levels depending on where they work in the body. Extreme changes in pH disrupt the ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the protein structure together, leading to denaturation.
bullets: Pepsin in the stomach works best at a very acidic pH of around 2.
Amylase in the mouth works best at a neutral pH around 7.
Too high or too low pH alters the active site shape.
Enzyme activity decreases rapidly when pH moves away from optimum.

callouts.p: pH curves look bell-shaped, just like temperature curves up to the optimum, but drop off due to changes in ionic bonding.

core.p: Enzymes lower the activation energy required for a chemical reaction to start. By bringing substrate molecules close together and correctly oriented in the active site, they make bond breaking and forming much easier.
bullets: Reduces the minimum energy needed for a reaction.
Reactions happen faster at lower temperatures than they would without enzymes.
Binding puts physical strain on substrate bonds.
Lowers the energy barrier on reaction profile diagrams.

callouts.p: Enzymes lower the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway.

core.p: Enzymes are widely used in industrial processes such as biological washing powders, food production, and pharmaceuticals. They operate at lower temperatures, saving energy and reducing costs.
bullets: Protease and lipase in washing powders break down protein and fat stains.
Isomerase turns glucose syrup into fructose syrup for sweeter drinks.
Carbohydrases convert starch into sugar syrups.
Operate at mild temperatures, reducing energy consumption.

callouts.p: Always mention lower operating temperatures and energy saving when asked about industrial enzyme benefits.

analogy.p: An enzyme is like a specific door lock, and the substrate is the unique key that fits into it. Only one key with the exact right cuts and grooves can turn the lock and open the door. Where this analogy breaks down is that locks are rigid and stay unchanged forever, whereas real enzyme active sites can sometimes undergo slight conformational shifts to grip the substrate even more tightly (induced fit), and enzymes participate actively in the chemical transformation before releasing the products.

terms.d: A biological catalyst, typically a protein, that speeds up metabolic reactions in living organisms.
The specific pocket on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The reactant molecule upon which an enzyme acts.
The molecules produced as a result of the enzyme-catalyzed reaction.
The temporary structure formed when a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site.
Describes an enzyme whose 3D structure and active site have been permanently altered, stopping function.
The temperature at which an enzyme exhibits its highest rate of activity.
The pH value at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.
The minimum energy required for a chemical reaction to start.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up or changed.
The characteristic whereby an enzyme catalyzes only one particular reaction or substrate.
The sum of all chemical reactions taking place within an organism.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are living things that can die.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are molecules, specifically proteins. They do not 'die'; they become denatured.

mistakes.w: Enzymes get used up during the reaction.
mistakes.r: Enzymes act as catalysts so they are regenerated completely at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: Any substrate can fit into any enzyme.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are highly specific; only a complementary substrate fits the active site.

mistakes.w: Cooling a denatured enzyme restores its shape.
mistakes.r: Denaturation is permanent; cooling will not reactivate a denatured enzyme.

mistakes.w: Enzymes provide heat to start reactions.
mistakes.r: Enzymes lower the activation energy, they do not supply thermal energy.

exam.q: What is an enzyme?
model: A biological catalyst
Made of protein / speeds up metabolic reactions
exam.tip: Learn standard definitions word for word.

exam.q: Explain why enzymes are specific to one substrate.
model: The active site has a specific shape
Only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit
exam.tip: Always mention the active site and complementary shape.

exam.q: Describe what happens to an enzyme at temperatures above its optimum.
model: Bonds holding the protein structure break
The shape of the active site changes / enzyme denatures
Substrate can no longer fit
exam.tip: Link temperature increase to bond breakage and active site shape change.

exam.q: Explain why lowering activation energy is important for living organisms.
model: Allows reactions to occur rapidly at normal body temperature
Without enzymes, reactions would be too slow to sustain life
exam.tip: Connect activation energy to body temperature conditions.

exam.q: Describe the lock and key model of enzyme action.
model: Substrate fits into the complementary active site of the enzyme
Forms an enzyme-substrate complex
Reaction takes place and products are released
exam.tip: Break the process into clear sequential stages.

exam.q: Suggest one advantage of using enzymes in washing powders compared to normal washing.
model: Can wash clothes at lower temperatures saving energy
exam.tip: Focus on energy saving and lower operating temperatures.

exam.q: Explain why pepsin in the stomach works best at pH 2.
model: Stomach contains hydrochloric acid creating acidic conditions
Pepsin's active site is adapted to function best at this low pH
exam.tip: Relate enzyme optimum pH to its biological location.

exam.q: A student claims that cold temperatures denature enzymes. Explain why this claim is incorrect.
model: Cold temperatures do not denature enzymes
They only reduce kinetic energy and collision frequency; activity resumes when warmed
exam.tip: Distinguish between temporary slow-down (cold) and permanent destruction (denaturation).

worked.q: An enzyme-catalysed reaction takes 40 seconds at 20°C and 10 seconds at 40°C. Calculate the percentage decrease in time taken.
steps: Find the change in time: 40 - 10 = 30 seconds.
Divide the change by the original time: 30 / 40 = 0.75.
Multiply by 100 to get the percentage: 0.75 * 100 = 75%.
